title: Lee's youth baseball team and why hustlers helped the kids
summary: Lee compares his father's fundraising to getting uniforms for his Los Angeles baseball team, helped mostly by gamblers like Black Dot McGee.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: So that's the way that they would get the facilities or whatever they needed to get -- whether it was uniforms or something like that, and it's just so strange the way history repeats itself, because I used to fool with kids here in Los Angeles, with baseball and basketball, and I remember one time that I had a baseball team, and we had 13 kids on the team and I wanted to get some uniforms for them, and you know, I'm speaking of Los Angeles -- and they had a lot of doctors and lawyers and professional people, and I think Alameda Davis had a paper called the Tribune, and she wrote in the Tribune that I had gotten these kids together and we needed uniforms and bats and balls and all that sort of thing ...

Well, I'll never forget that I only got 4 uniforms, and 3 of them were from for like, guys, like Black Dot McGee, and he gave one, and Sonny Howard gave one, and J.B. Brown, and then my father in law, Mr. Nelson, who owned the Dunbar Hotel; he gave one, but other than that, I had to pay for them myself.
So I guess, things don't change too drastically, you know?
Explain who Black Dot McGee was.
He was of the same ilk I was speaking of, you know, he was a hustler; he was a ...
He ran after hours joints, huh?

Yeah, he ran after hours places and J.B. Brown the same thing, and Sonny Howard, I think he had a pool-room --but guys who were in what they called the 'sporting life' you know? They were gamblers and they were hustlers, but it's something about them as far as the black people were concerned, they always seemed to help the youth more than the more educated people.

Now I guess you could say that was because they had it rougher and they knew they wanted to improve -- they didn't want the kids to have the same type of life that they had. That's what I always attributed it to, because I know that I would have to go to a place like Fontana and Black Dot would pick up some of the boys at 8 o'clock in the morning, and he'd been out all night and he would sleep in the car, while we were playing baseball, you know, but the professional people, they didn't seem to do that, so I was just trying to equate that with what my dad went through.
You know, many, many years prior to that, so I guess I'm saying I don't know how much we have improved.
